content:
Apple has asked the court hearing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to allow its own experts to access the forensic images used in the case, while also seeking documents related to OpenAI's hardware development. Details below.

Some background

In early July of this year, Apple sued a former employee, OpenAI, and io Products, accusing them of misappropriating trade secrets.

The lawsuit involves several former Apple employees who allegedly took confidential information with them when they left. Apple also alleges that former employee Chang Liu provided materials to study to another Apple employee before that person interviewed at OpenAI, while Tang Tan instructed job applicants coming to Apple to bring hardware components and other materials to their interviews.

Earlier, Apple said preliminary forensic examinations showed that a MacBook Liu used after leaving the company had been used during his time at OpenAI to run a simulation of an Apple-confidential circuit schematic. Apple also said the MacBook indicated Liu had used a Mac mini, which the company has subsequently sought to access as part of the case.

OpenAI later pushed back against Apple's allegations, claiming the situation was "a mess of Apple's own making," as the company said its offboarding procedures and security measures were handled too loosely, making it easier for employees to inadvertently retain access to confidential information after leaving.

One point of contention in the case is Apple's request for expedited discovery, which OpenAI opposes. Another is Apple's request for a preliminary injunction restricting OpenAI from using what it claims are Apple's trade secrets during the litigation, an order that could affect OpenAI's ongoing hardware development.

Apple argues it specifically needs expedited access to certain evidence because OpenAI is still developing hardware products, and any alleged use of Apple's trade secrets could become further entangled with that work, making it harder to undo later.

OpenAI, in turn, argued Apple has not shown why a separate expedited discovery process is needed, and said Apple's requests are overly broad.

With the parties at an impasse, the court ordered both sides to submit a joint statement outlining their respective positions on expedited discovery. The statement was filed last Friday and made public a few days ago.

Apple seeks forensic images and R&D materials

In the joint filing, Apple asked the court to allow its own forensic expert to access the underlying forensic images relied on by the defendants' expert to analyze Liu's devices and determine whether he accessed or used Apple confidential information after his departure.

Apple said one of its forensic experts had identified what it described as "material flaws" in the relevant analysis, and argued its expert needs to review them directly to determine whether the defendants' forensic analysis contains other issues.

Apple's statement follows:

Apple's forensic expert has identified several material flaws in the analysis performed by the defendants' expert, including: (1) failing to locate on Mr. Liu's Mac mini files that were clearly present and stored; and (2) incorrectly concluding that zero-byte files or empty kMDItemLastUsedDate fields on the Mac mini meant those files had not been accessed. [...] Allowing Apple's expert direct access to these forensic images is critical to understanding what other errors the defendants' expert may have made.

OpenAI argued Apple's expert should not be given unrestricted access to the forensic images, and instead proposed that a neutral forensic expert handle the images under a process agreed by both sides.

Apple argued this arrangement would put it at a disadvantage because the defendants' own forensic expert has already had direct access to the same materials.

Beyond the forensic materials, Apple is also seeking expedited access to documents related to OpenAI's hardware development, including R&D materials on metal surface finishes, power management, and battery functionality.

OpenAI had previously argued that its metal surface finishing was independently developed and did not use Apple's confidential information, and said the simulation Liu ran using Apple confidential files was unrelated to its upcoming products.

Apple is now seeking the underlying development records to verify OpenAI's claims; OpenAI says this is simply an attempt to "spy on a competitor."

The joint filing also addressed several other points of contention, including:

  • Apple's broader request for forensic images of devices used or previously used by Liu, Tan, former Apple employee Yu-Ting "Alyssa" Peng, and another OpenAI employee, containing or having contained what Apple defines as "Apple-derived materials";
  • Records of Liu's use of AI tools — defendants previously said the forensic investigation found no evidence Liu used Apple confidential files on platforms such as ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or OpenClaw;
  • Documents related to interviews at OpenAI's consumer hardware products division, including materials showing what was actually used in interviews at that division, and communications with departing Apple employees;
  • OpenAI indicated that written interrogatories to former Apple employees could potentially involve more than 400 current OpenAI employees.

Apple also sought the complete LINE conversation history between Liu and Peng, including exchanges in which Peng asked Liu technical questions about his work at Apple after Liu had left the company.

Defendants had previously submitted excerpts of those conversations in opposing Apple's motion for a preliminary injunction, but Apple argued it should be allowed to access the full conversation records, not just the messages defendants chose to submit.
